The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.

The Ollama CEO gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look nothing alike, and the real constraint on enterprise procurement is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver behind open models is control, not saving money
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is "better control over AI and customising it for yourself." Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once that is unlocked does it become about customising models to your own use case. The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting lever, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese ones.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
Ollama's cloud per-user token usage curve has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, support, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning an enormous number of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this surge.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to make sure it is fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the single biggest day of growth. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer and application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 Above the token is where the new scarcity lives
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgement: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B on top of those tokens. Following the path of cloud computing, developers ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than a packaged Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink down into the model layer
Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgement is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories cannot. One is state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolset the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 80% of tokens go through open models, but only 20% of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgement: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will go through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open source. The open community is driving cost extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spend lands on open models. The hardest work stays with the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is open and closed combined. He uses a law firm analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all
On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, face many hard problems, and rely mainly on large cloud models; end-to-end low-difficulty workflows like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve is extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Disappeared With Them
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is often written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years afterward no new Black medical school appeared.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is often written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years afterward no new Black medical school appeared.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological account of Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half, on how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a member of the medical profession. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording each one's admission requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave their patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admission standards were just as chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first and then graded school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than practising physicians doing this on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time teachers. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within a decade the number of American medical schools was down to half; the schools that survived reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised substantially. In Canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

23:43 He never did the arithmetic on Black medical schools' books
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven could "make no valuable contribution at this time," and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools," and said that one of the most important duties of Black doctors and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four closed before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school would not come until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school aimed primarily at Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966 and was a response to the Black community's need for access to care; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was an enormous care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's line about "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors had none.

26:51 The AMA was paying for the Carnegie project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for the project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There are also unresolved questions — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. His accounts differed over time; sometimes he said the man went with him, and later he changed his story to say they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was restricting Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains a passage of idealistic colour, saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions must "not directly or indirectly consider race, religion or sex." One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among their neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have led him to idealise the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for judging Flexner a racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's formulation may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he arrived at independently. In 2011, Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across racial divides — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Change One Law of Physics and Every Wish Backfires
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-skeptics-改一条物理定律-每个愿望都会反噬/
item.category: The Skeptics' Guide to the Universe
item.description: A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: you may change exactly one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity means free energy, hyperspace travel means handing the technology to every alien civilization.
item.content:encoded:
A live thought experiment from Dragon Con: you may change exactly one law of physics to make science fiction real, and every wish gets taken apart for the consequences nobody counted — antigravity means free energy, hyperspace travel means handing the technology to every alien civilization.

The first half is live-room riffing; the second half — the Roman telescope, robot babies, the falling-atom experiment on the Chinese space station and the Verne details — is denser and worth skipping ahead for.

2:07 Changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe
The rule is hard: pick exactly one, and it must be practical and feasible within the laws of physics — no perpetual-motion-style having it both ways. Steven starts by handing most science-fiction premises a death sentence — warp drive, shields, phasers, artificial gravity, antigravity — either they violate physics or they are non-trivial: theoretically maybe possible, but never going to happen. The real fun of the whole discussion isn't in what gets picked, it's in finding the consequences inside each wish that nobody counted.

8:08 Antigravity is free energy thrown in for free
Jay wants antigravity, on the grounds that transport, construction and materials handling would all change. Bob points out it's a twofer: if you can feasibly turn gravity off, then turn it on while the water wheel goes down and off while you haul it back up, and you've got a perpetual motion machine. Steven, as buzzkill, patches it by force: the energy consumed switching gravity off must equal the energy you get out of it, no free lunch. The argument also incidentally kills off science-fiction movies — single-stage-to-orbit is simply impossible in a 1g gravity well, and every shot of a ship reaching orbit in a minute is lying, because it assumes antigravity exists.

10:08 Hyperspace travel hands the technology to every alien civilization
Bob picks entering subspace/hyperspace: you travel under ordinary engines over there and come out having crossed a far greater distance, essentially practical FTL. He argues there's no downside risk, because hyperspace is separate from real space and doesn't affect our universe. Steven and Jay immediately push back: changing a law of physics changes it for the whole universe, not just for you, and hostile civilizations could use it to colonize Earth just as well. Bob's answer is to hide — human radio signals dilute into noise within a few light years, so in principle nobody can work backward from them to the fact that Earth has life. Jay offers a compromise, jump gates: both ends have to be built, so expansion can only be slow, and not every alien comes knocking.

23:16 Zero-point energy is too thin, and forcing it triggers a big rip
Steven's second choice is free energy, specifically zero-point energy. Bob gives the objection: zero-point energy is observationally extremely dilute, and lighting a single bulb might require several cubic light years of space; and if you really injected that much energy into space, cosmic expansion would run away into a big rip that destroys all life. Steven's response is that this is exactly why these aren't laws of physics — every wish, once it actually lands, brings catastrophic consequences, so the fun of the thought experiment is finding the loophole that dismantles the wish. Julia adds her astrophysics-major perspective: if gravity had a dial, 90% of the observations that infer stellar phenomena from gravity would all be wrecked.

36:19 A bucket of water can compute like a neural network
The core of physical reservoir computing: any nonlinear system — a bucket of swirling water, time-varying mayonnaise — as long as you measure the right spot, its nonlinear interactions can be mapped onto an artificial neural network and made to "think" for you. Someone gave a talk saying, "we got mayonnaise to think very slowly." Once that analogy holds, scale becomes a variable: if there were a nonlinear system the size of a nebula, you feed it input and measure output at the right point, and it does your computation for you. The speaker himself admits this is a "wild idea," but stresses that shrinking physical constants down to something tiny throws up a pile of strange corollaries.

44:29 Roman is a thousand times faster than Hubble, but cast as the supporting act
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a wide-field infrared telescope with a 3.4-meter primary mirror, the same size as Hubble, but its design goal isn't "better than existing telescopes" — it's complementary: James Webb excels at deep space, Hubble at staring at specific objects, Roman at taking in a huge swath of sky at once. It can survey a thousand times faster than Hubble, and over its five-year mission it will sweep an area of sky equivalent to a thousand years of Hubble. Once it finds something interesting, Webb and Hubble can be turned toward it for a closer look. It will also build a three-dimensional map of the universe and carries a coronagraph to block starlight glare and directly image exoplanets — it can find smaller planets farther from their host stars, offsetting the transit method's and radial velocity method's bias toward "hot Jupiters."

55:41 A robot baby kicks its legs and kicks up explore versus exploit
The University of Hamburg and Czech Technical University built a "robot in a crib": they put the infant robot iCub in a crib, hung a mobile with QR codes above it, tied one leg to it with a string, and ran their own deep learning algorithm to predict the mobile's motion. The result was that the algorithm spontaneously produced the explore versus exploit trade-off — being curious and exploring, but also exploiting the causality already learned. The researchers treat it as a platform: you can't change a baby's learning algorithm, but you can swap algorithms in a robot, so you can test different versions of contingent learning theory. By contrast, the mainstream of current robot control is deep reinforcement learning: put thousands of copies of the robot in simulation, train with a reward function, then transfer to the real machine in one shot — that's "do this and something good happens," not "this causes that."

1:04:44 China's space station redid the Leaning Tower experiment with rubidium atoms
On China's space station, researchers redid Galileo's falling-body experiment with two clouds of rubidium atoms of different isotopes, one heavier than the other. The free-fall time was about 10 to 12 seconds, far longer than in ground experiments, and averaging over many repeats, the two clouds fell at rates agreeing to five parts in ten million. What this verifies is that gravitational mass and inertial mass are exactly identical — in Newtonian mechanics mass shows up in two ways, and during a fall the two effects cancel precisely. What Einstein asked was precisely: why must they be the same? There is no reason they must be. From that comes his thought experiment: in free fall gravity seems to vanish and you are in an inertial reference frame; and in an accelerating elevator light bends, so if gravity and acceleration are equivalent, gravity should bend light too.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but Loops Only Climb to Local Optima
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.description: After prompts come agents, and after agents come loops. A loop will climb you to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.
item.content:encoded:
After prompts come agents, and after agents come loops. A loop will climb you to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.

Anish ties together agent deployment, model pricing, and the bottlenecks in consumer AI into one thread, and the second half — on moats and product questions — is worth more than the first.

0:00 Ideas that are too small get no funding now
Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would pass; today it is the reverse — ideas that are too small, too local, they do not want to touch. The reason is that model capabilities have torn down the ‘can it be done’ barrier, and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology ‘unbundling skill from desire’: not only can productivity be amplified, but so can the scale of what you want to do.

6:10 It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic
Anish pushes back on the ‘fast takeoff’ narrative: the people who understand it best in the labs do not say RSI (recursive self-improvement), they say autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own processes, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow; when he went back to his hometown he found people's lives had barely changed. Second, many problems are simply not intelligence bound — give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs and it will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush the competition.

8:16 Using AI and reorganizing around AI are two different things
Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to the actual reorganization of factories took 40 years, and it meant burning down old plants and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just give existing roles and functions access. He also cites the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone, including mechanics, to use the new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in a production environment.

11:18 Companies will become a series of nested loops
Anish's steel man: after prompts come agents (a loop of model plus tools, memory, skill files), and after agents come loops (a group of agents doing tasks). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and there is already a mature loop — bug reports come in, a reproduction is generated, it is fixed, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones go straight to production, and the customer is even automatically emailed. Above that there are loops per person, loops per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company.

14:18 A loop only climbs to a local optimum and stops
The growth team's version of a loop: every variant is automatically generated and automatically measured, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and ships, with a long-term holdout left in place, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish stresses that a loop will hit a local maximum and plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. His example is telling Claude ‘make me a million dollars, no mistakes allowed’ — it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

21:32 Frontier model pricing is actually irrational
Anish explains model choice with Pareto efficiency: frontier models are ‘irrationally priced’ on the price-performance curve — one more IQ point might cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries like drug discovery where the upside is unbounded, that one extra IQ point might be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; for work with bounded upside like law or finance, you just want Pareto efficiency and a cheap, good-enough open-weight model. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

31:46 People want to spend time, not save it
Anish says ‘loop, make me happier’ is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but actually they want to spend time — the world's biggest products are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: the AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly about whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; Instagram users just think ‘this is a better Google search’. He thinks this is not a model or capability problem, it is a product design problem: for the past 40 years we have built technology that extends the intellect, not something that extends the soul.

34:49 Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010
Anish compares the present to iPhone 2010 — Airbnb, WhatsApp, Uber had not appeared yet. Three things are holding back consumer: models are too expensive, making free products hard; the interface problem, chat only suits ‘the highest agency people in the world’ like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for ordinary consumers is TikTok, and we need to find something between chat and TikTok; and the technology has been too focused on productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models have brought costs down sharply, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interfaces, and Brian Chesky has also set up a lab focused on the next generation of interfaces.

item.title: Copper grades are falling from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand goes to infinity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding, new mines take 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding, new mines take 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland draws on 40 years in mining to lay out copper's supply-demand deadlock: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only come in the second half.

14:30 The next 18 years must mine all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get back roughly 700 million tons. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years must dig up the same amount of copper mined over the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is in freefall
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it has fallen to 0.8%, and within two years it will drop to 0.4%. Falling grade means crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding accounts for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search uses 30x the power of a normal search
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he cites ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30 times that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old in the world with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this very studio is itself copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell the acid to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply chain story absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and just the ring gear took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers trying to buy natural gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners earn $100 an hour; Congo engineers earn $800 a month
Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age of the population is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast if you don't invest, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest ever.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mines alive, but they'd stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly that he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.8, taking copper to $7.8, and then he can afford to pay American miners, making US mining viable. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher interest rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and nobody can tally supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says nobody can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on yen weakness so they never have to repay. He thinks we're at an inflection point, where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinizable.

item.title: A U.S. Measles Death Is Erased From CDC Data, and State Reporting Is Being Taken Over by the Federal Government
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.description: The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.
item.content:encoded:
The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the individual case: state reporting has become negotiable.

A clinical-update show: the first stretch is a quick pass over outbreak data, and the middle sections on the measles death dispute and the cardiovascular benefit of COVID vaccination are the densest, most worthwhile listening.

4:06 Local dengue has appeared in Florida
Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired cases, bringing the cumulative total to more than 70 locally acquired dengue cases, with 14 virus-positive mosquito pools detected across 5 counties. In the same segment he also mentions the health advisory the CDC issued that day — since July 2026, rabies-related consultations are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including mass exposure events, against a backdrop of U.S. pet owners becoming hesitant about vaccinating animals against rabies. Put together, these two things show not the sporadic appearance of some pathogen but that the United States has abandoned defenses against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that the NIH is seeking to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of research projects from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense program, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Defense Department response confirmed a research agreement had been signed, allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was reached in secret is false" — but the response never mentions the money. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Defense Department has plenty of money, and it does not need to reach into the pockets of an already underfunded NIH.

9:09 HPV vaccination has not risen in four years, at only 77.7%
The MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021, now stalled for a fourth straight year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose, and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the rural-urban gap for meningococcal vaccine appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can 100% prevent cervical cancer, anogenital cancers and head and neck cancers — why isn't it being done.

15:15 Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts
MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; each confirmed case identified on average only 10.6 contacts, against a target above 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases are occurring outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, when that number should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with a cumulative 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths.

17:16 The CDC removed state-reported measles deaths from the tally
On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday night, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying the available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key: state and local health departments do the case investigation, apply the case definition and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically has only received and aggregated, checking later. This time, though, the CDC was embedded in Pennsylvania's investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

19:18 No one routinely screens the dead for measles
A commentary in SIDRAP dismantles the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" argument: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance for clinicians is to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then mention testing. So when measles turns up positive in a death investigation, it is usually because there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes that the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but small enough that a rational person should shift their judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also became severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born without breathing and could not be resuscitated, with measles virus detected in lung tissue.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
Much of the dispute stems from how death certificates are structured, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part I lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line the immediate cause and the lines below it the conditions that produced it, and the last line the underlying cause that set off the whole sequence; Part II, in the words of the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate cause line says pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in Part II — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence that measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

24:20 The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases
Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury said in a STAT interview that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also disputed the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that, according to the Pennsylvania health commissioner, the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

item.title: The AI Doomer Narrative Is a Psyop, and the Target Is Open Source
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-allin-ai-末日论是场心理战-靶子是开源/
item.description: Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI could end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic asks public markets to underwrite it at a trillion-dollar valuation while its safety lead endorses the claim that AI could end civilization — not an internal contradiction, but regulatory groundwork aimed ultimately at open source.

The first half is a fight over Doomer PR and IPO disclosure; the second half's breakdown of OpenAI's math breakthrough and Nike's collapse is worth more.

0:00 The resignation letter wasn't spontaneous — it was organized PR
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic after only six weeks and posted that the people building AI genuinely believe it could kill everyone by the end of this decade. Sachs points out this wasn't spontaneous: the account had almost zero followers and zero posts before, yet got hundreds of millions of views in a day; within the first 15 minutes three Doomer organizations amplified it, all funded by the same big EA donor, who also co-led Anthropic's Series A. More tellingly, the Wall Street Journal story went out minutes before the tweetstorm — meaning the reporter had been briefed under embargo. Sachs says if Coxon really came on the show, the first question would be: who introduced you to the Wall Street Journal?

6:12 The company didn't distance itself — it amplified him
A normal company would immediately push back and distance itself from a whistleblower. Anthropic did the opposite: Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment, publicly replied that Jacob is right, that they genuinely do believe AI could kill all of humanity, and that he personally puts the probability at over 10% in the next decade. Sachs argues this exposes the contradiction — what he said matches the company's internal Doomer agenda exactly, which is why he got internal support. Chamath adds the knife: the company can't distance itself, because the moment it does, that whole internal bloc blows up.

10:18 Asking for a trillion-dollar valuation while saying the product could end civilization
Sachs lays out Anthropic's IPO dilemma clearly: you're asking public-market investors to underwrite your company at a trillion-dollar valuation while your safety lead says the core product is unsolved and could end civilization. That is at minimum the seedbed of product-liability litigation. Chamath uses the Philip Morris analogy: we know cigarettes kill you, we'll say so, but we won't disclose it, we'll still list and let you buy the stock, and we'll figure it out later. Sachs calls it "a time for choosing" — either publicly deny that Coxon is a Doomer operation, or admit Bernie Sanders is right and development should be frozen, in which case how do you IPO at a trillion-dollar valuation?

22:45 The real target of regulation is open source
Sachs is blunt: this is a Doomer psyop, and the end goal is open source. Because FDA-style regulation won't say "ban open source" — it will say open and closed models are subject to the same standards — and Dario has already testified in the Senate that models are dangerous if they can't be centrally monitored and rolled back. Once open-model weights are released they can't be rolled back, so the standard landing means banning the release, use and hosting of those weights. Freeberg adds: open source has no corporate structure to file regulatory paperwork, and open source is exactly what cut AI costs 50x and benefits everyone. Chamath's version: once open source is banned, you get a monopoly working hand in glove with the federal government.

39:17 AI can't even nail autocomplete yet
The core anti-Doomer argument isn't theoretical — it's everyday experience: autocomplete still isn't good, and AI can't even handle the trivial task of carrying a toiletry bag upstairs. If it can't finish one mundane task, why believe it can kill all of humanity? They call this humanity's insurance against AI taking over the world — company decisions still require humans to wake up, drink coffee and sit in the same room, and there is a natural 16-hour window between decisions.

50:45 What's truly damning is that retweet endorsement
From a legal standpoint, the key isn't Jacob Coxson's resignation tweet — it's Evan Hubinger's endorsement retweet. He is still a senior alignment executive at the company, running one of the safety teams, and his co-sign plus the "greater than 10% probability" figure is what made it go viral. If it were only Coxson, the company could call him a disgruntled employee; but an executive endorsement turns "was disclosure adequate" into a real question.

1:00:12 OpenAI solved the math problem with brute force, not divine inspiration
The Navier-Stokes solution used roughly 130 billion output tokens, with 10,000 agents communicating with each other, equivalent to between 50,000 and 500,000 years of human work (estimated at 40 words per minute of typing). AI had no flash of insight humans couldn't have — it just did a massive amount of brute-force work, and every step of the message chain is logged and readable by humans. The conclusion: AI is a leverage tool, not a math god standing above people.

1:15:40 De-identification doesn't remove the method itself
De-identification can strip personal information and company-specific information, but the general method for solving a math problem is itself IP. A user iterates on that method inside the tool, and that conversation can be de-identified and used for training, making the model better at math. That's the network effect of closed models: they can see what the whole world is doing, and this observation system feeds them more data than anyone else, which is a long-term advantage over customers.

item.title: Active management giant moves its headquarters to Nashville, saving $85 million a year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.description: Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and it did not force a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and personnel costs, and the bet is on hiring people New York cannot.
item.content:encoded:
Alliance Bernstein relocated from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and it did not force a single portfolio manager to move — the savings come from real estate and personnel costs, and the bet is on hiring people New York cannot.

A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401ks. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

9:18 When passive squeezes active, cut costs before talking growth
The Alliance Bernstein Bernstein took over was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions falling from 20 to 25 cents a share all the way to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — the merged AUM had touched nearly $900 billion mid-quarter, and by 2012 only $380 billion remained; in 2006 roughly 70% was equity assets, and by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced part of the teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and an emphasis on distribution.

21:39 Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year, with no forced relocations
The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being that it wanted to be a big fish in a small pond, which it could not do in Charlotte or Dallas. The move saves roughly $85 million a year, part real estate and part personnel. The key design: no portfolio manager was forced to move, because the firm is a price-taker for that kind of talent. As a result, nearly 100 portfolio managers moved voluntarily. The challenges are concrete too: Nashville is the capital of the healthcare services industry, and locally it is hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training; but the firm received a flood of résumés from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

25:44 Sell-side research without cross-subsidy can only be a joint venture
Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Nearly every peer uses equity capital markets or prime brokerage to cross-subsidize its research department, and Alliance Bernstein had no such businesses to subsidize with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition entirely to SocGen. He specifically mentions the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Britons — so it had to be advanced step by step, very carefully. The transition period runs five years from the JV's anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

37:08 Banks are structurally unsuited to holding long-dated fixed-rate assets
Bernstein uses his experience doing leveraged finance at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players operating on short funding, structurally unsuited to holding long-duration, especially fixed-rate, assets. JPMorgan at the time spent a great deal of time and money trying to securitize its loan book, and credit derivatives started there. Insurance companies and funds are a better home for these assets, because funds do not offer a genuine liquidity option and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that there is no maturity transformation in credit, and apart from interest and principal there should never be any liquidity at all.

40:14 Private credit's problem is not defaults, it is insufficient disclosure
Asked how the industry gets past the troubles of the first half of this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure obligation, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and one should "over-communicate in times like these." He also frames the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are simply the normal state of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; what went wrong was a handful of companies, plus fraud, which has always existed; what genuinely went wrong was that structure and pricing got out of balance for a time. His conclusion is that after going through this, now is actually a better entry point.

43:14 Private credit in 401ks: fees are not the obstacle
Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401ks may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlisle to develop a vehicle that can be used alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He concedes the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years, but in ten years it will most likely be part of large plans. On the objection about fees, his response is: these are institutional buyers and they will bargain hard; and private assets are only a small part of a target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

47:18 Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at it
Bernstein cites Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and that one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at it. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mostly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people have not saved enough to retire, and will delay retirement and look for supplemental income. He also proposes a specific mechanism: rather than buying an annuity in one lump sum at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income security over a longer lifespan.

51:26 AB is the last publicly traded partnership
Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits their willingness to hold the stock. He describes the stock as "a bond with an equity option," essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure and give the stock a pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock did not pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is that it is not a sure thing.

item.title: AI 2040 Isn't About Stopping AI — It's About Pushing Superintelligence to 2040
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-tbpn-ai-2040-不是停掉-ai-是把超级智能推迟到-2040/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-tbpn-ai-2040-不是停掉-ai-是把超级智能推迟到-2040/
item.description: The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute cap: pause new frontier training, allow only inference, and make weight theft impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.
item.content:encoded:
The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute cap: pause new frontier training, allow only inference, and make weight theft impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.

High information density, but the topics jump around: AI regulation, robotics, how VCs read people, and the chip supply chain each get a segment — good for listening selectively.

0:00 AI 2040 doesn't stop AI, it delays it to 2040
Many people assume anti-AI sentiment is pushing to ‘stop AI’, but what the AI 2040 proposal actually says is: keep inference on existing models, keep doing capability research, and just push superintelligence from 2028 to 2040. The concrete mechanism is a compute cap — pause new frontier training, apply ‘inference-only verification’ to data centers above 10,000 H100-equivalents (roughly $100 million of equipment), and physically rip out the high-bandwidth east-west networking inside the data center so distributed training can't run but inference proceeds as normal. New R&D centers would have to be built from scratch inside a Faraday cage, with external connectivity capped at 1 MB/s — stealing the weights would take five years.

0:00 Anti-AI mobilization is nowhere near anti-battery-chicken
Speaker 2 points out a contrast: the anti-flock (anti-battery-chicken) movement converts into real physical action by ordinary people, whereas on the anti-AI side you don't see a hundred-thousand-like video teaching you ‘how to cut power to your local data center’. Speaker 1 adds that the volume on the anti-AI side comes more from concrete self-interest — ‘I'm an artist, I don't like AI-generated images’ — than from x-risk arguments. Data centers sit in remote locations, behind fences, heavily fortified, far harder to get at than a chicken coop on the street.

0:00 The compute cap is the valve easiest to turn
The most effective control lever in the proposal is judged to be the compute cap: chip controls plus slower data center construction. The goal is to make models stronger mainly by adding hardware rather than by new algorithms — because algorithmic breakthroughs can be hidden inside secret projects. Speaker 1 notes that Ilya's new lab recently got a large cluster from NVIDIA; even people taking an orthogonal research path have to stack compute, which suggests ‘scale is the precondition’ is basically consensus in this circle.

0:00 Doomists don't bet, because they wouldn't live to collect
Tyler Cowen demands that pessimists name the corresponding market price to validate their belief, but Deep Dish pushes back: why should a short-term existential risk be reflected in market prices? ‘If everyone's dead, the contract that pays out is worthless to me.’ Speaker 5 twists the knife: in the nuclear-war era people built bunkers; nobody builds an AI bunker, because everyone thinks it's too totalizing for a bunker to help — so ‘you didn't build a bunker’ doesn't prove you don't believe. Paul Christiano was dug up as being 2x levered long and short 30-year US Treasuries, but that bet also makes money in the ‘good ending’, unlike a doomsday wager.

0:00 The fruit fly agent moves the moral question forward
Google mapped every neuron of the fruit fly, and once the code was open-sourced people started messing with it in every way: someone put the fruit fly agent inside a Rabbit R1, and shaking the device makes its escape circuit light up; someone else made it play Doom. Speaker 1 thinks the real question is the next stop on this road — if you can simulate a human, hold a conversation, behave like a human, does it have moral status? His own judgment is not to overthink it, and not to be in the business of torturing anything. He also mentions that last night he had Astra play Balatro using computer use, and it felt like giving it a reward rather than torturing it.

0:00 Once a reporter is in the room, he stops being escorted out
Alex Heath describes the core mechanism of his changed status: when a reporter is in the room, you're brought in and then immediately escorted out; now he gets to stay in the room and slowly marinate on it. So his newsletter perspective changes — it's not about landing a scoop, but about letting a large volume of off-the-record conversation settle into a judgment, like the personal agents piece he's writing. He says explicitly that confidentiality still matters, and he won't leak a memo a company is worried about again — ten years in, that's enough.

0:00 A newcomer can hardly replicate his path now
Asked whether now is a good time to become the next Alex Heath, his answer is the opposite: the traditional media environment is structurally challenged, many places aren't hiring, traffic is falling, and they haven't shifted to direct models like subscriptions and streaming. The only viable path he offers is ‘maniacally focus on one thing and become the best in the world at that’ — he himself started by focusing on covering Snap, broke a pile of Snap news, and once noticed, migrated that capability to other companies. And the niche has to be the intersection of niche and matters, not just obscure.

0:00 Fear of being left behind hands new players an opening
A host other than Mitesh offers a counterintuitive mechanism: because people fear AI, they're more willing to try new products — they don't want to be left behind, don't want to become a permanent underclass. The result is that people who have used various AI products for years are still willing to try new things, which keeps creating an advantage for second and third entrants. At the same time, once an AI brand gets big it starts accumulating baggage, and people become more willing to share and discuss something new rather than the one they use every day. That leaves a lot of room for startups.

item.title: The Oldest Manuscript of the Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performance Copy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.description: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
item.content:encoded:
The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.

This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

1:03 The most complete version is an English manuscript
The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France proper — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was at some point bound together with a completely unrelated book, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Who bound them together is unknown; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

3:05 Every stanza is a camera position
The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut in performance into four plus six: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

7:27 At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially violent or the emotion especially strong, several consecutive laisses will tell the same action from three angles, a kind of slow motion in verse. Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant, for instance, is told three times with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — "Roland dies, his soul ascends" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

9:29 The performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript
Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will not tell more." This line comes before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem and is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

10:31 Pocket-size dimensions give away that it was a tool of the trade
The manuscript measures only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket copy you could carry on your person, not a rich man's finely bound volume. It is itself heavily worn and not fine, and contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to an itinerant professional performer: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator of a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical acting. Such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler.

12:31 The dialect pins this performer to England
The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor of the continent, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests this performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant and l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French is also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

14:34 Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
Scholars' grip on this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound.

17:40 A French epic, an English artefact
Although this is a French poem about an old French king, the manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no equally complete manuscript to compare it against line by line, but there are abundant records of the Song of Roland being sung before and after this copy, and from these scholars can judge where this performer departs from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience is constructed, and what the music sounds like.

item.title: The Army Secretary Resigns: The People Who Know How to Fight Get Cleared Out First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risks are being purged batch by batch.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risks are being purged batch by batch.

The first half — 9/11 reflection and Army personnel insider detail — is dense; the second half, on AI battlefields and model distillation, is more casual chat, so you can listen to just the first half.

3:03 The war on terror ate the money for military transformation
Before 9/11 the US military was pursuing transformation as Rumsfeld demanded, under the expectation of a relatively comfortable budget environment in which new technology could be folded into the force gradually. Then GWAT arrived, all available resources were sucked into the war, and the transformation directive remained while the money was gone. The result was a run of procurement disasters: the Army's Future Combat Systems, the Navy's Ford-class carrier, the Littoral Combat Ship, DDG-1000 Zumwalt, and the CGX that was simply never built. Brian's judgment is that the technology jumped too far ahead, the investment was nowhere near enough, and everyone was distracted supporting a war that had just started, so these programs were doomed. The troubles with today's B-21 and F-35 trace back to this period too.

5:22 Twenty-five years on a treadmill, never actually stopping
Tony points out that op-tempo never stopped after it started in 2001: 12-month and 15-month deployment rotations, with the National Guard still deploying at home and abroad today. Killing Bin Laden in 2011 could have been a high point, but nothing changed afterward — deployments continued, and through the fall of Kabul, they were still deploying. No one has fully calculated what 25 straight years in that state costs an army. Brian adds a mechanism: conventional forces used to train at home, reset, and move through a training progression, and that rhythm disappeared, replaced by "preparing for the next deployment," so there is no time to test new technology or study new ways of fighting.

7:31 MRAP thinking: use a bigger truck to stop an anti-tank missile
Brian gives an example absurd in its specificity. In Syria the threat was not IEDs but ATGMs (anti-tank guided weapons, similar to Russian TOW variants). The commander's reflex was still to stuff everyone into MRAPs — making the vehicles bigger, which made them easier for ATGMs to spot, while MRAP armor cannot stop munitions designed to penetrate tanks. His conclusion: risk calculation in the war-on-terror era has gone so deep that commanders cannot reconceptualize even a small tactical adjustment. This is also the direct consequence of why so many commanders today struggle to adapt to Ukraine and the Lisko battlefield, and cannot imagine how tactics will change.

9:37 Get used to zero casualties and you can't accept dying
Brian says that after 9/11 the US military became increasingly risk- and casualty-averse. The Littoral Combat Ship debate is the specimen: opponents said the ship couldn't take a hit and would be sunk the moment war started; the original proposers answered that it was never going to be sent into a major war, and if it got ambushed and sunk, that was the risk you take for serving. That logic was completely unacceptable on Capitol Hill — Iraq and Afghanistan pushed casualties far below the levels of past wars, everyone got used to it, and so they cannot accept that against a peer opponent a great many people will probably die. The result is continued construction of "Death Star"-style big ships and big platforms, expected to protect themselves, rather than a route toward smaller, more distributed forces that accept a different risk structure.

10:39 Twenty-five years surrounding Iran, but no network built
Brian says this is the most important lesson he took from 9/11, and it came from a friend's reminder: for 25 years the US has essentially surrounded Iran, and the CIA's and part of special operations' job is to develop networks and identify people who could oppose an oppressive regime, in case a moment of change comes. But when the shooting against Iran started six months ago, it looked like very little network and capability building had been done in those 25 years. The reason is a mental shift: GWAT focused on counterinsurgency and catching bad guys, not the long-term unconventional warfare of pre-positioning for future conflict — how to support an insurgency inside a regime you might one day want to overthrow. In his words, everyone was too busy stabilizing the situation rather than destabilizing.

13:53 Driscoll resigns, and from here on it's all acting officials
Tony recaps: George was relieved, Driscoll went to the White House, said "everything is terrible," and resigned that same week. The backdrop is the Army being meddled with back and forth by OSD and the Secretary of the Army's office, plus personality clashes. What he hears is that Congress will not confirm anyone else Pete nominates, so either they bring in someone both the White House and Congress can accept but Pete doesn't like, or they just keep using acting officials. He judges this is the start of the rest of this administration being "stuck with acting officials": after the midterms the House flips at least, the Senate either flips or goes 50:50, no one has the energy to push this kind of nominee through, so acting officials, continued OSD meddling, and low morale will persist.

14:54 The drone battalion is disbanded, and the ability to experiment goes with it
The Army decided around the same time to dissolve its newly created drone battalion — a battalion meant to absorb Ukraine's experience directly and then study how to embed it into infantry battalions. Tony concedes there is a good argument that "it shouldn't exist in just one battalion": concentrating lessons in a central repository strips every commander of the responsibility to think about force organization themselves. But his worry is that the Army still needs a unit that can run experiments, run tests, and allow failure; cutting it in the name of "uniformity" loses the ability to experiment, and the force will stand still. He also names Chris Donahue as sacrificed: a commander widely recognized as understanding technology, its effects, and how to run international partnerships, done in over the Abbey Gate bombing (not his fault) and a photo a reporter took.

21:03 Confidence is lost in layers, by rank
Tony breaks morale down by rank: junior officers are still early but already thinking "garrison isn't what I signed up for," and if not garrison then it's going out to get hit by missiles; field-grade officers are starting to agonize over whether they have to make political decisions just to stay; senior field-grade officers and junior generals are basically "all in or burned out." He says the whole force is tired, and this doesn't look like the Army they joined. And in interviewees' telling, the Iran war is more of a tipping point than Donahue's departure — many O-4s and O-5s he knows originally supported this administration and are furious after the Donahue affair. Brian adds: people like Donahue are the true product of elite selection, and cutting them makes people doubt the claim that promotion is "by ability alone."

item.title: AI researchers sped up 10x in two years, but RSI may be easier than being a paralegal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
item.description: RSI is a cumulative task — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember constantly shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things: a non-stationary distribution.
item.content:encoded:
RSI is a cumulative task — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember constantly shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things: a non-stationary distribution.

The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning and RL generalisation are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of the episode.

0:00 A model looks smart, then a month later it looks dumb again
John Schulman describes a recurring loop: a new model comes out, people are blown away, they say "this is AGI", but after about a month of use it starts to look dumb again. The loop may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. His mechanism: capability won't explode right now, because when doing research and engineering you still get stuck on bottlenecks — even if a model can write far more code than a human, that doesn't give you a 100x productivity gain. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if by 2036 there's no crazy alien superintelligence, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec-paradox-style continuation — AI does superbly at whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but a stubborn sim-to-real gap always blocks the rest.

18:39 Distillation is the only force against centralisation
John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralisation trend: anything learnable through RL can be distilled easily, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices.
